hints.content:
The graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=-3\sqrt[3]{-x}-5$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ and $g(x)=-3\sqrt[3]{-x}-5$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=\sqrt[3]{x}\\\\
f(-x)&=\sqrt[3]{-x}\\\\
-3f(-x)&=-3\sqrt[3]{-x}\\\\
-3f(-x)-5&=-3\sqrt[3]{-x}-5\\\\
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $g(x)=-3f(-x)-5$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $-x$ reflects the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ over the $y$-axis.


[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its horizontal reflection graph on an x y coordinate plane. Its middle point is at (zero, zero). It passes through (negative eight, negative two) and (eight, two). The reflected graph has its middle point at (zero, zero). It passes through (eight, negative two) and (negative eight, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $\sqrt[3]{-x}$ by $-3$ reflects the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{-x}$ across the $x$-axis and stretches it vertically by a factor of $3$.


[[☃ image 1]]

Note that graph of the function passes through $(8,-2)$ *before* the transformation, and $(8, 6 )$ *after* the transformation.  This is because each $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $-3$.

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its transformed graph on an x y coordinate plane. Its middle point is at (zero, zero). It passes through (eight, negative two) and (negative eight, two). The transformed graph is vertically reflected has its middle point at (zero, zero). It passes through (eight, six) and (negative eight, negative six).

hints.content:
Adding $-5$ to the function shifts the graph of $y=-3\sqrt[3]{-x}$ down $5$ units.


[[☃ image 1]]

Note that it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

If we shift the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.


[[☃ image 1]]

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

[[☃ image 2]]

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, negative two) and passes through (ten, negative five).

The shifted graph has its middle point at (zero, negative five). It passes through (eight, one) and (negative eight, negative eleven).
